analysis.one_liner: Requires big corporations getting COVID-19 federal aid to give employees annual stock grants until the aid is repaid.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced in May 2020 with zero cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 bailout wave, this bill would have required large publicly traded companies that take federal rescue money to share ownership with their workers. Every year while the aid was outstanding, the company would have to grant employees stock equal to at least its typical annual stock grant percentage, with shares going out on a formula weighted toward lower-paid, longer-serving workers. Executives and big owners would be excluded, and the shares would carry full voting and dividend rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Rank-and-file employees of large corporations that receive federal COVID-19 aid: they would receive free shares of company stock, weighted toward lower salaries and longer tenure, with no requirement to buy anything or meet performance targets. The shares would carry the company's highest voting and dividend rights, and the bill states the grants should not replace any existing wages or benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Each year while federal COVID-19 aid is outstanding, a covered corporation must grant employees whole shares of stock equal to at least its average annual stock-and-option grant percentage over the three years before 2020 [S3].

Individual grants are weighted by salary with a wage cap of $137,700 and by tenure, so lower-paid, longer-serving workers get proportionally more, and executives, managers, and anyone owning over 5% of voting shares are excluded [S3].

The grants cannot be conditioned on buying company stock or on performance evaluations, must carry the highest voting and dividend rights the company issues, and Congress states they should not substitute for any existing wages or benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The covered corporations and their shareholders: they would have to dilute ownership by issuing shares to employees for as long as federal aid remains outstanding. Executives and large shareholders are excluded from receiving the grants. Companies that repaid their federal aid promptly would owe nothing under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to any publicly traded company receiving federal aid, including loan guarantees and Federal Reserve emergency lending, so a company taking even temporary support faces multi-year dilution of its shareholders until repayment, which could discourage firms from accepting aid in a crisis [S3].

Employees receiving stock in a single bailed-out company would have their wealth and possibly their voice tied to that one employer's fortunes, a risk employee-ownership critics have long noted (general knowledge about concentrated stock risk).
The requirement is defined by the company's own past stock-grant levels, so companies that never granted much stock would owe workers very little under the formula [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real but bounded: it converts bailout-era corporate support into a modest employee-ownership stake rather than new cash, and the formula scales with each company's past practices, so it is more a fairness condition on rescue money than a broad wealth-sharing program. The costs fall on shareholders of aid-receiving companies, which is the intended trade-off, though the single-stock risk for workers and the potential chilling effect on taking emergency aid are legitimate concerns.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on May 13, 2020, during the COVID-19 rescue debate [S1].
No member cosponsored it, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day [S4].
The committee never acted on it; the bill's only actions were introduction and referral, and it expired with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that received federal COVID-19 aid and their shareholders came out ahead: no condition requiring them to share ownership with employees was ever enacted, while workers at those companies received no equity benefit.

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring equity grants to employees of corporations receiving COVID-19 federal aid.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No other member signed on from either party, so the bill never drew enough support to reveal how the parties would have split on a vote.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid
industries.note: They would have had to issue stock to their rank-and-file employees, diluting shareholders, for as long as federal aid remained outstanding. Companies could avoid the obligation only by repaying the aid.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and large shareholders of aid recipients
industries.note: They are explicitly excluded from the grants and would bear the dilution cost of shares issued to other employees.

industries.industry: Federal Reserve and Treasury emergency lending programs
industries.note: The bill lets corporations use federal aid to finance leveraged Employee Stock Ownership Plans, tying rescue lending to employee-ownership structures for the first time.
